title: QDC 2026: what quantum developers need to know
content: Quantum Research Blog QDC 2026: what quantum developers need to know A developer’s guide to the hardware, software, and workflows unveiled at IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026. Date 11 Nov 2026 Authors Genya Crossman Sanskriti Deva Robert Davis Topics Enablement Error Correction & Mitigation Software Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 (QDC 2026) unveiled a wave of new Qiskit tools for developers, spanning hardware, error correction, workloads, applications, and access. IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2, the fastest processor yet, gives developers direct pulse-level control for building, running, and iterating on frontier quantum circuits. New error-correction tooling lets developers build with fault-tolerant primitives today, from stabilizer-code frameworks to long-running repetition-code experiments on real IBM Quantum hardware. The directed execution model and new managed workflows on IBM Quantum Platform give developers more control while scaling across quantum and high-performance classical computing. Expanded application tooling connects real problems in chemistry, materials, and optimization to quantum circuits, turning verified quantum advantage into practical workflows. Every release pairs with IBM Quantum docs, tutorials, and runnable Qiskit code, plus new AI agent skills and expanded free access to start building. Quantum advantage is increasingly a developer experience, not just a research milestone. That transition was on full display at IBM Quantum Developer Conference 2026 (QDC 2026), which showcased the practical tools that help developers build, test, optimize, and scale quantum workloads today. Across the event, IBM highlighted a growing portfolio of Qiskit-based and community-driven tooling for exploring industry applications, contributing to open source, building production-ready workflows, and academic research. In this post, we’ll walk you through the releases that matter most for developers across hardware, software, error correction, and access—and we’ll show you how to get started building with each. High-performance hardware for frontier circuits For developers, everything starts with the hardware. This year, a big jump in speed made it easier than ever to build, run, and iterate on frontier quantum circuits that test the limits of our capabilities. IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 — developer capabilities Our fastest processor (120 programmable qubits, up to 100,000 samples/sec), with pulse-level access developers can use directly: mid-circuit measurement, fast qubit reset, dynamic circuits, and soft (IQ) readout. Why it matters: The speed and real-time control that make frontier circuits practical, plus the hooks to test error-correction techniques on real hardware today. Get started: Read the Nighthawk r2 blog and run circuits today on IBM Quantum Platform. See what Nighthawk can do with our onset of ergodicity tutorial , which runs and analyzes a 64-qubit experiment on a Nighthawk processor. Code: Speed is what lets you explore frontier circuits at scale—and you don't have to take our word for it. IBM's device benchmarks are all public, so you can measure a processor's max circuits per second (MCPS) yourself. from qiskit_ibm_runtime import QiskitRuntimeService from qiskit_device_benchmarking.mcps.mcps_benchmark import MCPSBenchmark service = QiskitRuntimeService() bench = MCPSBenchmark(service, "ibm_nighthawk") # your backend name print(bench.mcps()) # e.g. {'mcps': ..., 'num_circuits': 1000, 'shots': 1000, 'total_time_seconds': ...} Copy to clipboard For a more hands-on test, the mirror benchmark runs a utility-scale circuit and checks its accuracy—part of IBM's fully open benchmarking suite (MCPS, CLOPS, EPLG, and more). Enabling error correction research Error correction was one of the most important themes at QDC 2026, with the quantum team showcasing an expanded error-correction stack. This included new developer tooling that lets developers begin working with the concepts, workflows, and abstractions that will underpin future error-corrected systems. These tools are part of an integrated suite that spans the full stack. Alongside error-correction frameworks like Qiskit Paulice, you'll find modular error-mitigation tools— qiskit-mitigation and qiskit-noise-learning —covered later in this post in the “running and scaling workloads” section. Qiskit Paulice A framework supporting stabilizer-based computations and quantum error-correction workflows (spacetime codes for Clifford circuits). Why it matters: Lets developers and researchers start building with the primitives of fault-tolerant quantum computing today. Get started: Read the Paulice blog , explore the docs , or work through the spacetime-codes tutorial on IBM Quantum Platform. Code: Here's the core workflow—adding spacetime checks to a Clifford circuit to improve the fidelity of its measured distribution: pip install qiskit-paulice from qiskit import Quant
